newsitem.title: UK: U.S. oil stocks firm in London, but Dow seen weak.
newsitem.headline: U.S. oil stocks firm in London, but Dow seen weak.

text.p: Tracking strong gains in oil shares worldwide, U.S. oil stocks rose in London following news the U.S. launched an attack on air defence targets in Iraq.

But traders here said they expect the broad U.S. market to open sharply lower after the Wall Street Journal, quoting unnamed Federal Reserve officials, said policy makers were considering a larger-than-expected 0.5 percent hike in the fed funds rate.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the policy-making arm of the Fed, meets again on September 24.
The Dow, closed yesterday for a U.S. holiday, could open with as much as a 30 point loss, traders said. The leading stock average settled at 5,616.21 on Friday.
"All (trading) has been confined to oil," a London trader said of this morning's activitry. "Oil stocks will temper the fall. If it weren't for (firm oil stocks), the Dow might open 40 points lower."

Shares in Texaco and Chevron each gained $3/4 in London to $89-1/2 and $59-5/8, respectively. Shares in Amoco climbed $1/2 to $69-1/2, while Exxon firmed $5/8 to $82. Texaco, Chevron and Exxon are all components of the Dow.
Crude oil prices were higher in London, as well. Brent was up $0.50 per barrel at $22.49 in late morning trading, extending Monday's $1.21 gain on Monday.
In other trading, the September S&P 500 futures contract was down 3.80 points at 647.55 on Globex at 1040 GMT. The September 30-year Treasury bond futures contract was off 4/32 at 107-6/32.
A report on U.S. leading economic indicators for July, due for release at 1230 GMT, could have a modest impact on the market at the open, traders said.
The National Association of Purchasing Managers index for August, to be released at 1400 GMT, could influence trading later in the U.S. session, they said.
However, the focus for U.S. financial markets remains on the August employment report, to be published on Friday. That is widely seen as key indicator of U.S. monetary policy.
